name: NAD+ injections

lead: NAD+ is a coenzyme every cell uses for metabolism. Some clinics sell injections or infusions of it for anti-aging, energy and recovery, and people use it hoping for fresher skin and a more youthful look.

NAD+ carries electrons in metabolic reactions and is used by sirtuin, PARP and CD38 enzymes. Proponents say injecting it raises levels that fall with age; reference sources note that human evidence for that decline is inconsistent. Registered human trials of injectable NAD+ address specific medical conditions such as hematopoietic recovery, hearing loss and vascular aging.

paras: It is given at wellness and longevity clinics as an injection or an IV infusion, often as part of a broader anti-aging or energy package. Users describe it as a periodic treatment and report effects on energy and how they feel.

Experts quoted in reference works say the long-term safety of intravenous NAD+ is unknown. It is not licensed as a medicine in the UK. Clinic marketing claims for aging and appearance have not been tested in controlled human trials.

angle.text: Longevity clinics and online communities promote injected NAD+ to raise cellular NAD+ levels, with the aim of better cellular energy and repair and fresher, more youthful-looking skin. The appearance claim rests on cell biology and user reports; registered human trials address other conditions.

lead: NAD+ injections are parenteral (injected or infused) preparations of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, a coenzyme found in all living cells. They are marketed by some wellness and longevity clinics, and discussed online, as an anti-aging or energy-boosting treatment.[1][1]

NAD+ itself is a well-characterised molecule central to cellular metabolism. The claim that raising NAD+ by injection slows aging or improves appearance is a separate question, and no controlled human trial of injected NAD+ for appearance or aging was found. Registered human trials of injectable NAD+ (often called coenzyme I in Chinese registrations) address other conditions, such as hematopoietic recovery, hearing loss and vascular aging.[2][3]
In the United Kingdom, NAD+ is not licensed as a medicine, and experts quoted in reference works say the long-term safety of intravenous NAD+ is unknown.[1]
infobox: Not licensed as a medicine in the UK;[1] varies elsewhere

paras: A heat-stable yeast factor that accelerated fermentation was reported by Arthur Harden and William Young in 1906, and its role in hydride transfer was shown by Otto Warburg in 1936.[1] NAD+ carries electrons in redox reactions and is also consumed by enzymes such as sirtuins, PARPs and CD38.[1]

Researchers have proposed that falling NAD+ levels contribute to aging, but the encyclopedia record notes that evidence for age-related NAD+ decline in humans is inconsistent, and that a 2024 rat study reporting such a decline was withdrawn after image manipulation was found.[1]

sections.h: Use in longevity and wellness clinics
paras: Clinics offer NAD+ infusions or injections for energy, cognition, recovery and anti-aging. In the UK, high-cost infusions have been marketed for alcohol and drug dependence, and the reference record states there is no proof such treatments work.[1]

No controlled trials of injected NAD+ for skin, appearance or healthy aging outcomes were found. A registered trial (NCT06919328) is comparing absorption and tolerability of an injectable nicotinamide riboside product with NAD+ in healthy aging, but no results were located.[2]

Other registered trials of injectable NAD+ concern hematopoietic recovery after cord blood transplant, sudden sensorineural hearing loss, immune thrombocytopenia, vascular aging and pediatric cardiac dysfunction; these are small and mostly early phase, and are not studies of appearance.[3][4][5][6]
Published laboratory work includes a 2025 mouse study in which NAD+ attenuated demyelination in an autoimmune encephalomyelitis model.[7]
Experts cited in reference works say the long-term safety of intravenous NAD+ is unknown.[1] No safety data from controlled trials of cosmetic or longevity use were found.

timeline.event: Harden and Young report the yeast 'coferment' later identified as NAD.[1]
Warburg shows NAD's role in hydride transfer.[1]
Sirtuins discovered, later linked to NAD+ aging hypotheses.[1]
